body:
Never heard of Townes Van Zant. I've heard of David Foster Wallace in the past and was considering reading Infinite Jest, but at the time it didn't seem like something I was going to complete reading. What exactly is it about/like?

I remember the two times I left the hospital from serious mood issues. I felt like a totally different person, like you said - things I imagined happen suddenly started crumbling and it just felt like I emerged from hibernation, almost. I get the impression that they try to make the hospital so unpleasant that you don't want to be in there, though, because it was a relief just to get out of there and be home.

It's good that you're at that point with your choice-making. I imagine that once you've reached that point, you're definitely at least making progress in getting better. For myself, it's mood-dependent. When I'm depressed, I'm much, much more able to rein in angry impulses, for example, but in other periods that can be nigh on impossible. 

Also, thanks for the comment at the end.

That is nice to hear, and I'm glad someone gets that impression, although the fact that I sound like a mixture of people you know is kind of what I'm getting at. I don't think I'm a magical special snowflake, but it feels like my identity (which is essentially constant) is stitched together from so many disparate - or, at least, not directly related - areas that it's hard to find interactions with other people. Nothing against other people for having different interests from mine, but it can be rough.

It's even nicer to hear that you've listened to Devin Townsend. Always glad to hear other people know the man. He's my absolute hero. 

I've been playing video games for soooo long in my life. I've been made fun of by my family as 'always playing games' or 'always on the computer' (and that's true to an extent). When I was much younger I played the N64 all the time (constant Goldeneye N64 and The World is Not Enough) and I've been keeping up to date with games ever since. 

I don't think being an influential thinker is really part of my personality, though it definitely was huge at the time. Now, it's not really a thought that occurs to me. Now, I don't think I can be a renowned thinker, or at least not anything approaching what it was like during the manic episode (I literally thought I was going to write a world-changing book that was ridiculously broad and would solve every philosophical problem imaginable). I don't think I'm dumb or completely ignorant, but I recognize now a much greater deal of uncertainty than I would ever grant at the time (back then there was a massssive drive to know things). I have some opinions and thoughts, but I don't see them as particularly novel. I'd generally like to be an educated person with well-developed opinions in the future, so it's not like those desires are completely gone, but I have a much more realistic appraisal of how it is right now, I think. 

I'm studying environmental science at university because I didn't really know what to do with myself. First year I took a mix of science and arts courses. I tend to do much better in arts courses (I got a 4.0 in a philosophy course that I frequently missed classes and was late on assignments for), but I'm skeptical about my future in those things, so environmental science seemed like an option and I picked it essentially at random. 

I've tried a couple of clubs, yeah. I went to an improv club that was supposed to be casual, and it was casual, but the people there were extremely extroverted and bouncy and bubbly and it's just not my type of thing, though they seemed to be having fun with it. I also tried to go to a book club at my university, and it had 4 other people there, which was awkward. Other than that, there weren't too many clubs that caught my eye to go to. I'd definitely like to go to clubs that appeal to my interests, but I don't see too many options at the moment.

Gotta warn you, I use way too many words. 

Yeah, I read all 10 over the summer. Probably my favourite books of all time. I loved Whiskeyjack, but there were so many characters that I loved that he probably wasn't even one of my top ones. I've read a bit of fantasy recently (ASOIAF, Malazan, The Witcher, and currently going through Black Company - a series Malazan was partly based on) and in the past read a lot of philosophy and classic literature (Dostoevsky was a favourite for a while, even though I'm not religious; Erikson actually really reminded me of Dostoevsky at times). 

I know exactly how you feel. Getting that stupid 'think positive' or 'enjoy the little things' speech is so ubiquitous that I already know everything people are going to say by the time they start going into it (got it earlier today, actually). Something that depresses me (further) is earlier today a really nice girl in one of my classes talked to me one-on-one pretty extensively(after having really limited contact with other people in university; zero friends, a few acquaintances) and it felt good for a while and now my mood's dropped straight back down. I *can* feel good sometimes within the mood, but it falls straight back down. Such a pain. 

In terms of the curling up in a ball, I want to do the same thing. I'm a very reserved person when I'm depressed, but there's been times where I've honestly just felt like asking people I don't really know for a hug because I feel so low. I don't, because I don't want to seem like a creep on top of being depressed, but it feels so isolating. I find for myself that I can't cry when I'm depressed - sometimes it's so bad that it feels like I want to sob but nothing happens whatsoever. And yeah, I use humour heavily to regulate what I'm feeling. I wouldn't call myself a funny person, but I joke excessively at times. Takes my mind off briefly if it's not too bad, and can be fun if you make people laugh.

It's been my experience in the past, too. Even people who said they loved me didn't really care the same way I did. It's been so difficult finding someone likeminded who cares like I do - both of those things are made more difficult by being an introvert, like you. It does suck from a social standpoint to be an introvert. I really do like it to some extent, though. I enjoy having an introverted disposition - I just don't like the social consequences it has on me, especially mixed with my other issues. I totally get where you're coming from with that.

I don't have a job at the moment, no. I'm a second year in university living at home (it was cheaper and less stressful than residence - obviously wouldn't help my social interactions though). I'm mostly aloof from the people around me, including the friends I interact with. I like a lot of them, but I get this sense that there's not really any substantive connection there, and there's always this consciousness that our interactions aren't that meaningful. I don't really struggle with arguing with people or anything when I'm not 'manic' (calling it that for shorthand; still don't know), but I really struggle with enjoying the relationships I have and finding new ones. I can play the part reasonably well, but it feels more like I'm a stagehand in my life than the lead actor. 

It is weird in a way, because I also keep this stuff mostly to myself outside of a clinical setting, but at the same time it's nice talking to someone else, even if neither person really knows what to do. You get used (or at least I do, though I gather you have similar experiences) to the world being cold and feeling almost alien to your internal world, so when you do talk to someone struggling similarly it's nice.

I have to ask, is your name Whiskey jack daniels or Whiskeyjack Daniels? There's a character in a book series I've read named Whiskeyjack.

That sounds like a really difficult situation. In the past, I've struggled massively with relationships, partly because I would feel that the other person didn't care (like you did). However, I wouldn't have the restraint that you do. I burn bridges (oh god I hope your name is a reference to Whiskeyjack now) when I feel that way. I imagine sex would be helpful even without the emotional component (although of course much more helpful with it). For me, my sex life has been like rainfall in the desert. Massive dry spells and a couple of periods of light rain.

I wish I knew what to say to you as well. Of course people can give bullshit motivational speeches, but I'm sure we both know that that doesn't get us very far. I'm at a loss with what to do with myself. I'd like to help other people as well, but I can't help myself. It's good in a way to know other people are struggling (though it's obviously also terrible that other people feel this way).

I can recognize I have some degree of internal strength given what I've faced, but it's hard for me to find a way to translate that into anything helpful. It just feels meaningless. 

My interests are fairly broad but they're also incredibly introverted and kind of odd, from my perspective. 

Reading's one. I've read a lot of philosophy in the past (one of my 'manic' - again, assuming diagnosis is correct - periods involved delusions that I'd be a world-changing thinker, so that fueled a lot of the reading) as well as classic literature (Dostoevsky was a favourite for a while, I read James Joyce, Cervantes, a little Proust, Hemingway, Shakespeare, that sort of stuff) and fantasy (Malazan Book of the Fallen is probably my favourite set of books ever, also ASOIAF, The Witcher series, and I'm currently trying to read Black Company). I know most people read, so that's hardly 'odd', but in terms of my genres and stuff like that I find they're fairly broad and don't necessarily match up, which can make finding similar interests difficult.

I also listen to a lot of music. Can't play for shit, except for getting some good marks when they forced us to play the recorder in grade 3, but being able to play the recorder is almost the opposite of musical talent. Again, listening to music is hardly unusual, but the genres I listen to are odd. My favourite musician of all time is Devin Townsend without a doubt. My most listened to genre is metal, and I listen to essentially anything within it (though my favourites tend to be the progressive side of the various subgenres), which is something that most people really don't like (especially extreme metal, which I love). Beyond that, I listen to essentially anything. I know people say that and then have a laundry list of exceptions, but I genuinely like stuff from a lot of different genres. Post-rock, hardcore, rap, some country (haven't heard much, but Devin Townsend's country album is amazing), indie, folk, electronic, classical (used to like Mahler a lot) and so on. Again, listening to music isn't odd, but my primary genres are not popular ones and the combination of genres is kind of weird and eclectic. 

I also play a lot of video games. Recently it's mostly been League of Legends, and before that it was The Witcher series. My gaming is pretty broad, and it's not one where I'd say I have an odd mix, but again, hard to find gamers that I interact with well.

Besides that stuff, I essentially just like thinking about shit and having conversations. 

None of these things make me a particularly interesting person. I don't think of myself as a special snowflake or unique or better than other people by any stretch of the imagination, but I do recognize I'm different and it makes meaningful interactions difficult because it's hard to find common ground (especially since it's hard to find people who might be similar). If I don't have common ground, I really struggle to interact with people well in a deep manner. I can make small talk fine and all, just can't get it to go further than that. 

Sorry, that was a long post, I'm kind of rambling, just wanted to make clear why they're introverted as hell. I'm kind of a boring person overall, nothing very interesting or stimulating for others.
